claims.title: Shopper order details may be intercepted if storefront transport encryption is not verified
claims.description: `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` to the internet-facing `process:storefront-api` and carries order contents, shipping addresses, and card last-four data. Its `encryption_in_transit` state is unknown; if the flow is not protected by TLS, an on-path observer on the public-network route can intercept shoppers' PII and financial order details. Second-order, the captured shopper identifiers and order information can be correlated to target shoppers or their orders through later interactions with `process:storefront-api`. This is conditional on the unresolved transport-encryption attribute, not an assertion that the traffic is plaintext.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses the public-internet boundary and has unknown transport encryption, but interception requires an on-path position. Impact is high because the flow carries both `pii` and `financial` assets, including shipping addresses and card last-four data.

mitigations.summary: Verify and enforce TLS for shopper checkout traffic
mitigations.detail: Set and continuously verify `encryption_in_transit` for `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` as TLS 1.2+ with modern certificate validation; redirect or reject non-TLS requests.

mitigations.summary: Minimize payment-related fields in the order submission
mitigations.detail: Avoid carrying payment-related values beyond what checkout requires and use opaque order references where downstream components can resolve the details.

claims.title: Settlement status may be intercepted if webhook transport encryption is unverified
claims.description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` into `process:storefront-api`, carries a financial settlement confirmation, and has unknown protocol and `encryption_in_transit`. If the callback is not protected in transit, an on-path observer can intercept payment-settlement information for orders handled by the storefront. Second-order, settlement status and order correlation data can help an attacker target paid orders or craft more convincing payment-related fraud. This is conditional on the unresolved transport posture.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because the webhook crosses the public-internet boundary and its protocol and transport encryption are unknown, while exploitation still requires an on-path position. Impact is medium because the flow is tagged `financial` and reveals settlement state, but the modeled payload is a settlement confirmation rather than the full order corpus.

mitigations.detail: Document and enforce TLS 1.2+ for `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook`, including certificate validation at the callback sender and receiver.
Use an opaque payment or order reference in the callback and retrieve any additional settlement detail only over an authenticated protected channel.

claims.title: Order data may be readable on the storefront-to-core gRPC path
claims.description: `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` crosses from `boundary:storefront-dmz` to `boundary:core-services` and carries order contents, shopper identifiers, and shipping addresses. Although the flow has no authentication, this disclosure threat concerns its separate unresolved `encryption_in_transit` state: if gRPC transport protection is absent, an attacker able to observe the DMZ-to-core path can intercept PII and financial order data. Second-order, the shopper identifiers and order details can be used to correlate records subsequently persisted through `process:order-service` to `store:orders-db`. This is conditional on the unknown encryption attribute.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because the flow crosses from `boundary:storefront-dmz` to `boundary:core-services` with encryption unverified, though the attacker must obtain an on-path foothold. Impact is high because the flow carries `pii` and `financial` assets, including shopper identifiers and shipping addresses.

mitigations.summary: Use mutually authenticated TLS for gRPC
mitigations.detail: Set `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` to mTLS so both confidentiality and service-peer verification are enforced across the zone crossing.

mitigations.summary: Reduce sensitive fields forwarded to the order service
mitigations.detail: Pass an opaque order reference where possible, allowing `process:order-service` to retrieve only the fields it needs through its authorized data path.

claims.title: Orders database traffic may disclose shopper records if internal transport encryption is absent
claims.description: `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` carries order rows, shipping addresses, and card last-four data between `process:order-service` and confidential `store:orders-db`, but both its protocol and `encryption_in_transit` state are unknown. If this database connection is not encrypted, an attacker with an internal network observation point can intercept PII and financial records as the service reads or writes them. Second-order, captured rows reveal the data structure and shopper-to-order mapping needed to target records or customers in later attacks. This draft is conditional on the unverified transport control.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because transport protection on `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` is unknown, while an attacker still needs an internal on-path foothold. Impact is high because `store:orders-db` is confidential and the flow carries `pii` and `financial` data including shipping addresses and card last-four.

mitigations.detail: Require TLS with certificate validation for `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` and fail closed when encrypted transport cannot be negotiated.
Limit connectivity to `store:orders-db` to the necessary workload identity and private path, reducing who can obtain an observation point even if a transport configuration regresses.

claims.title: Receipt contents may be intercepted while conflicting transport records remain unresolved
claims.description: `flow:process:order-service>store:receipt-archive>append-receipt` writes receipt content identifying an order and the writing service to `store:receipt-archive`. The System Model records `encryption_in_transit` as absent, while the evidence catalog records that source material states TLS and that the sources disagree. Until that conflict is resolved, an on-path attacker on the service-to-archive path may be able to intercept receipt data. Second-order, accumulated receipt metadata can reveal completed-order activity and relationships between order records and `process:order-service`; this is a conditional finding, not a conclusion that TLS is absent.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because the transport evidence for `flow:process:order-service>store:receipt-archive>append-receipt` is explicitly conflicting, and exploitation requires an on-path position. Impact is medium because receipt content records completed-order activity and the flow is associated with `business-critical-data`.

mitigations.summary: Resolve and enforce the receipt-upload TLS posture
mitigations.detail: Reconcile the conflicting transport records, then require TLS with endpoint certificate validation for `flow:process:order-service>store:receipt-archive>append-receipt` and test that plaintext upload is rejected.
Avoid transmitting unnecessary customer or order detail in receipt object names and payload metadata; use opaque receipt identifiers where feasible.

claims.title: A copied orders database may expose confidential shopper and payment data if at-rest encryption is absent
claims.description: `store:orders-db` is classified confidential, holds `pii` and `financial` assets, and has unknown `encryption_at_rest`. If the unresolved attribute means storage encryption is not enabled, an attacker who obtains a decommissioned volume, snapshot, backup, or other storage-layer copy can read order rows, shopper addresses, and card last-four values without using the application read path. Second-order, the copy provides a corpus-scale shopper-to-order mapping that can support targeted fraud and privacy attacks. This claim is conditional on the unknown at-rest encryption state.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because `store:orders-db` has unknown `encryption_at_rest`, and storage copies can be accessed independently of the application even though obtaining one requires access to storage operations. Impact is high because the store is classified confidential and tagged `pii` and `financial`, including shopper addresses and card last-four data.

mitigations.summary: Verify and enforce encryption at rest for orders data and copies
mitigations.detail: Establish the actual `encryption_at_rest` posture for `store:orders-db`, then use managed or customer-controlled keys for the primary store and every backup, snapshot, replica, and decommissioned-media workflow.

mitigations.summary: Restrict storage export and key use
mitigations.detail: Limit who can create or retrieve database exports and backups, and separate key-use permission from routine database administration where possible.

claims.title: Receipt archive copies may disclose completed-order records if its at-rest encryption posture is unresolved
claims.description: `store:receipt-archive` holds receipt records for completed orders. The System Model records encryption at rest as absent, but the evidence catalog says the source material states a customer-managed key and that the sources disagree. Until the conflict is resolved, an attacker holding an archive backup, exported object copy, or other storage-layer artifact may read receipt records without using `process:order-service` or the archive's normal authorization path. Second-order, those receipts expose completed-order activity and can be correlated with order data held by `store:orders-db`. This is conditional because the stated at-rest control is contradictory.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because the storage-encryption evidence for `store:receipt-archive` is explicitly conflicting and a storage copy must first be obtained. Impact is medium because the archive holds completed-order receipt records, although its `data_classification` is unknown and it is tagged `business-critical-data` rather than customer PII or credentials.

mitigations.summary: Reconcile the archive encryption evidence and cover operational copies
mitigations.detail: Verify whether `store:receipt-archive` uses the claimed customer-managed key, correct the model to the verified state, and require the same protection for object versions, backups, exports, and replicated copies.

mitigations.summary: Restrict archive and key access separately
mitigations.detail: Use least-privilege archive-reader roles and restrict customer-managed-key decrypt permission to the minimal service and recovery principals.

claims.title: Code in the order service can read the full orders corpus through its broad application account
claims.description: `process:order-service` reads and writes `store:orders-db` through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`, and the application account is stated to have full read/write on the database. An attacker who gains code execution in `process:order-service` can use that service's standing database access to read the entire orders corpus, including shopper addresses and card last-four data, rather than being limited to the order currently being handled. The account password is also held in an environment variable on the worker, increasing the sensitive authority present in the component. Second-order, corpus-scale records allow correlation of shoppers, addresses, and completed orders; at-rest encryption would not prevent reads performed through this authorized database session.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low because the attacker must first gain code execution in internal `process:order-service`; however, the stated application account and password custody make the resulting read authority directly available once that foothold exists. Impact is high because the account has full read/write on confidential `store:orders-db`, which holds `pii` and `financial` order records.

mitigations.summary: Reduce the order service database grant
mitigations.detail: Replace the full read/write application account with narrowly scoped roles, tables, columns, and operations required by `process:order-service`, separating routine writes from broad reporting reads.

Use workload identity or short-lived database credentials issued through a dedicated secret manager, and prevent environment dumps and diagnostic output from revealing database authentication material.
Log database access under a distinct service identity and alert on query volume, table access, or export behavior inconsistent with normal order processing.
